text: 282. Words for cuckoo (or ‘cuckoo’ sounding words designating other birds) are certainly onomatopoeic. But this knockout argument does not mean too much. Within the northwestern and a few other Outer Languages they can be divided into a few groups, in this way disclosing some typological relationships. Note also that some languages have more than one word for ‘cuckoo’. (a) The OIA kokilá- type. The words of this group have not lost the medial -k- just like their Dravidian parallels: Pal. kaˈkūli ‘cuckoo’, Bhad. kākoli ‘cuckoo’ (Kaul [2006 i: 107]), Kaul also gives with- out further West Pahāṛī language specification (2006 i: 32) gaḍkākoli ‘cuckoo of the rivulet’ (but 2006 ii: 395 he says it is from Bhal. meaning ‘pakṣī viśeṣ – type of bird’); in vol. i p. 187 there is the additional alloform Bhal. gaḍ kagholi (with first syllable < OIA *gaḍḍa-¹ ‘hole’ [3981] and note k – gh alternation); there is also the Bng. cuss pũnskōklɔ ‘flatterer, idiot, blockhead’ which cf. with S. kokiḍī ‘stupid as a fowl’; Him. koklā ‘the blackbird’, N. kokʌle ‘cuckoo’ (Z.) and Western Nepal shamanic language kokalsārī ‘cuckoo’ — K. kukilü ‘cuckoo’, Ind. kʌkuìlⁱ ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. káku, kúku ‘cuckoo’ (but note also p. 792 Bur. kápo ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. kíki ‘falcon’) – Ko. koguḷ ‘cuckoo’. Cf. OIA kokilá- ‘cuckoo’ (3483), kukubha- ‘the wild cock Phasianus gallus’ (3210), *kūkkati ‘screams’ (3390), DN: 21 kokk-, kukk- ‘call’ and PMK *kuk, kuuk ‘to call’, but more significant are semantically close Dravidian parallels: Kan. kukil ‘cuckoo’, Tu. kogilè, kojilè ‘cuckoo’, etc. (b) The kuku type which does not have close Dravidian parallels: Kiũṭh. kūkū ‘cuckoo’, Jaun. kūkhū ‘cuckoo’, N. kukku ‘cuckoo’— K. kuku ‘cuckoo’ — Bhaṭ. bã̄kükú ‘type of brown-coloured pheasant’ with first component < vána-¹ ‘forest’ (11258) resembles K. van-kŏkürü ‘a kind of wild bird resembling a barndoor fowl’ but both may rather contain the word for ‘hen’ — Gau. kukʰ ‘type of woodpecker’, Bur.ys. kúku ‘cuckoo’, Kho. káku ‘cuckoo’ and narkˈuku ‘rooster’ (with first syllable < OIA nára- ‘male’ [6970]) — Jaṭ. kak ‘large hill partidge’ — Yid. kakūk ‘cuckoo’. Cf. PIE *kukū ‘cuckoo’. (c) kuku with other extensions: Sutlej Group koklas ‘type of pheasant’ (Malhans [2002: 262]) and Sh.dras. kʌ́kəs ‘pheasant’ (Rajapurohit [2012: 43]) are probably built on the kokilá- basis with vāśuka- element like other ‘pheasant’ words in the northwest (see p. 648 and Aw. kaṭnās ‘a kind of bird [? a jay]’ which may be a case of semantic-morphological amalgamation [on this term see p. 224]). N. kākākul ‘a part. kind of bird’ has a close parallel in Nuristani Kt. kúku kuli ‘cuckoo’ (cf. OIA *kululi- ‘outcry’ [3347]). Kal. kokḍúm ‘cuckoo-like bird’, Kho. kokdˈum ‘coocoo’ (‘cuckoo’) with unclear second component. Rp. kəkcilāṛu ‘a black chicken-like bird’ is a synonym compound: cf. Bng. ċilāṛ ‘cuckoo’ with first syllable < OIA cilli- ‘a kind of bird of prey’ (4829) and Jaun. bhūĩ̄-cīl ‘pheasant’ (with first word < OIA bhú̄mi- ‘earth, ground’ [9557]). More unclear are Psht. kūkūkūtarah ‘a ringdove’ (probably kūkū plus kotar ‘pigeon’), and Mult. and P. kakuhā ‘sandpiper’.

text: 302. Garh. karõco ‘fish trap’ < OIA (Pañcat.) kūṭaracana- ‘a laid trap’ which cf. with Kann. khuröṅċ ‘leopard trap’ ; here perhaps also Wg. köv a mesh of branches for catching fish’ without the Indian racana- extension and which is < OIA (R.) kūṭa-⁸ ‘trap for catching deer’ (3397). The CDIAL lemma has reflexes in Pk. and S. to which I add Bng. kuṛiāṇɔ ‘to pursue, chase’ (with -a-, -ā- suffix). According to Mayrhofer, kūṭa-⁸ is probably a borrowing from Dravidian as found e.g. in Kan. gūḍu ‘trap for catching wild animals’. Note also similar sounding OIA matsya-karaṇḍa- ‘a fish-basket, any hamper or receptacle for fish’ built with OIA káraṇḍa-¹ ‘basket’ (2792).

text: 519. (a) Bng. cəś ‘burning pain’, Kc. ċaśiṇo ‘to be burnt (e.g. hand on hot iron)’, Deog. and Jaun. ciśṇɔ ‘to burn one’s hand etc.’, Him. cośṇu ‘to burn with fire’, P. cīs ‘a sharp pain’, Ku. ciśṇō ‘to burn’, ciśi ‘scare of fire’ and cis ‘keen pain, scorching’, cisuk ‘very cold’, N. ciso ‘wet, cold’, Kgr. cas ‘slipped disc’ — Ind. c̣ʌ̀ṣ ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain; lumbago; a touch’ and c̣ʌ̀s ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain’, Kal. čičiék ‘to burn or smart (as salt in a wound)’. The words are to be seen in connection (i) with OIA *cassakk- ‘throb, twitch, sudden pain’ (4730), *cīssa- ‘sharp pain’ (4847), caṣati² ‘hurts’ (4727a), chaṣati ‘hurts’ (Dhātup.) (the aspirated form is reflected in Garh. chasāk ‘nukīlī vastu kī halkī cubhan - slight sting or piercing through a pointed object’), cahakk- ‘burn brightly’ (4731) (with debuccalisation), and perhaps cāṣa-  ‘sugarcane’ (4774) (see there G. cās ‘boiled syrup’), and (ii) with OIA *atyuṣati ‘burns’, *atyoṣati, *atyuṣyate ‘is burnt’ (226a), and (iii) perhaps with Dravidian DEDR kiccu (1514): Tam. kiccu ‘fire’, Tel. ciccu ‘fire, flame’ etc. which is perhaps worth comparing with Garh.nā. cac-kār, cac-gār ‘very cold’ (with -kār suffix). The Bng. and Deog. forms go back to older *c̣aṣ-, but not the Kc. form which therefore must be an early borrowing at a time when Proto-Bangāṇī and Proto-Deogārī still had three sibilants but Proto-Kocī only two. See next and next but one. (b) Like in the preceding paragraph, also in this paragraph semantic-morphological amalgamations (see p. 224) have been rampant. Bng. jàṣṇɔ ‘to singe s.o. (e.g., with an iron rod)’, invol. jàśiṇɔ, jìśaiṇɔ ‘to singe o.s. badly’ (with -ai- suffix), Garh. jhās ‘slight neuralgia or birth pangs’, jhasāk ‘touch through fire or nettle’ and jhusmus ‘dawn, early morning’ — here also A. zah ‘heat, summer’? — Pal. jhāṣˈī ‘caterpillar’ (contact with some types causes severe allergic reactions), Tor. j̣eṣ ([jyɛṣ]) ‘caterpillar’, K. zᵃj ‘a certain tiny longish insect, similar to an ant, which by coṅtact with the skin causes irritation and scratching’, Dari. jhusili kirā ‘caterpillar’ and Garh. jhissu or jhijju ‘ek roẽdār kīṛā – a hairy worm’ and jhusalyā ‘person with unwanted hair on his face or body’ and Kho. ǰaláṣ ‘hairy (person); a disheveled, long-haired person’ derive either/or or both < OIA lex. jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359) or < OIA *adhyuṣyate ‘is lighted up, burnt’ (280a) with a modern reflex in Kṭg. There is also Bng. ujà̄śɔ n.m. ‘the power that induces spontaneous possession (e.g., during the approaching of a deity towards a village); splendour of the sun’ (with retention of palatal feature because of coronal consonant harmony) which is < related OIA *ujjhāṣa- ‘shining’ (1678) (Pk.) with one modern parallel in G. to which is to be added Br.-Aw. ujās ‘light; gleam’, and Bng. jà̄ś n.f. ‘tension, stress, impulse, cheering up’ which also derives < OIA lex. *jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359). (c) Bng. kiśaiṇɔ or ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch children in jest with glowing charcoal’ (the lat- ter form is apparently cognate with forms listed in paragraph [a]), Khaś. kreśśnū ͡ and Bhad. ṭlessnū ‘cries due to physical pain’ (Kaul [2006 i: 305]) < OIA *kreśayati ‘presses’ (3606) (but regarding semantics compare cognate OIA kleśayati ‘torments’) with a modern parallel in Dm., but the verb has further parallels in Roh. (3588), Kal. (3589), K. (3590, 3591) and Wg. (3605). Notes: (a) Despite the massive semantic-morphological amalgamations one wonders whether above alternation of Bng. kiśaiṇɔ ∼ ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch . . . with glow- ing charcoal’ does not indicate a reflex of OIA KĀŚ ‘shine, look brilliant’ which may be also reflected in Bng. cɔṣṇɔ ‘to light, ignite, burn s.th. or s.o.’, cɔśkɔ i.a. ‘a sudden and short apparition (e.g. of a ghost or of a god in a medium)’ and perhaps in cɔkśɔ, cɔkśelɔ ‘shining, radiant’ if this is reflex of older *caśaka-(illa-) (extended with -kɔ2 suffix [and MIA -illa- suffix). In such a case it could be morphologically compared with OIA cáṣṭe ‘appears’. This interpretations seems semantically more plausible than borrowing from Dravidian. (b) The same OIA root in form of cākṣuṣá- ‘relating to sight’ is perhaps the origin of Kal. čákaš ‘cowrie shell’ which, regarding basic meaning, cf. with Kal. čákaš čhína ‘animal with white mark on its face’ (with second word < OIA cihna- ‘mark, sign’ [4833] and aspiration fronting).

text: 868. Pr. nü-lüšt ‘woman; mother and daughter; the women of a household’ is a synonym compound < OIA lex. nayaná-² ‘pupil of eye’ (6968) with meanings ‘beloved girl, pretty girl; wife’ in varieties of West Pahāṛī and in Nepālī ‘darling’ plus < OIA duhitŕ̥- ‘daughter’ (6481); the synonym compound has, however, an exact parallel in Bhaṭ. nã̄-kᵛüṭ̚ ‘girl’ which is ← Bhaṭ. nǟ́ ‘wife’ plus < a sideform of *kuḍa-¹ (3245), cf. Tam. kuṭṭi ‘young girl’ (DED 1390).

text: 1244. Bng. mɔ̄ḷṇɔ, mɔḷmɔḷaṇɔ, ‘to glitter’ and miḷmiḷaṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker (as light); to flash (lightning)’, kɔḷmɔḷi adj. and kɔḷmɔḷī n.f. ‘burning (as a sensation); shining, sparkling; shine, lustre, sparkle’ and here perhaps umbḷɛ̄ṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker, waver (e.g., a fire, swarm of flies)’ (with -ɛ-, ɛ̄- suffix). The reduplicated form is found, e.g., in the PAN, describing the ‘flickering’ (i.e. light emitting) crown of King Duryodhana, e.g.: raza Duriodən kɔ barthɛ kɔ mukuṭ mɔḷmɔḷa King Duryodhana GEN.POP stately.OBL GEN.POP crown flickers ‘The stately crown of King Duryodhana flickers’[318] Cf. OIA (AV) kalmali- ‘splendour, brightness, sparkling’ and OIA malmalābhávant- ‘flashing, glittering’. For kalmali- Chandrasekaran (p. 41) suggests Dravidian origin, e.g. found in Tam. mallal ‘elegance, brilliance’, which cannot be the source for the Bng. word, but for which Bomhard suggests PN origin (< *mal-a ‘fullness’ [CINCL 847]). Mayrhofer says about malmalābhávant- (EWA II: 333) with reference to Karl Hoff- mann that the word is ‘sound symbolic rendering of a (visual?) impression (‘Gesichts- eindruck’) through repetitive onomatopoeia’, but Chandrasekaran (p. 42) suggests also for this word Dravidian origin and he quotes as parallels Parji melk- ‘to lighten’, malk- ‘(light) to flash’ and Pengo malkā- ‘to lighten’ (p. 41) which, however, have parallels in Indo-Aryan Ḍog. milk ‘lightning’, Dari. milkala ‘lightning’, N. milkinu ‘(of the sky) to flash with lightning’ and most variants of Ind. ˈmili ‘lightning’ (Hallberg [1992: 211]; Leitner [1889: appendix iv, 14]), Gau. milyõ ‘lightning’, K. vuzmal and Sir.ḍoḍ. uz- muliˈya ‘lightning’ (both are synonym compounds with first component (v)uz- < OIA vidyút- ‘flashing, lightning’ [11742]), and Tibeto-Burman Khm. milak ‘flash, flash of lightning’ and Western Tibetan Balt. melmel ci ‘a very small indistinct glow (of light)’. There is also the H. ideophone milmilānā ‘shine, shimmer, glitter’ (Kellersmann [2017: 609]). Thus, derivation < PIE *(s)mel- ‘give off light smoke, smoulder’ and possible contamination by ‘sound symbolic’ word forms is rather unlikely. Still, if the OIA form can be characterized as ‘repetitive onomatopoeia’ one wonders that it survived unchanged over millennia in a comparatively small area. Note also that the Bng. poet. word barthɔ ‘stately’ is hardly < OIA bhártr̥- ‘husband’ etc. (9402), displaying a rightward displacement of aspiration but rather cognate with bharatá-. However, cf. Pischel § 207 who mentions OIA suffix -tha instead of -ta in M., AMg., JM. Bhāraha. Note also Martirosyan’s perhaps related reconstruction (2013: 112) PIE *mar- mar- reflected in dialectal Arm. *mar-m(a)r-il ‘to shimmer, flicker, glimmer, ex- tinguish gradually (said of e.g. a candle)’ and Greek μαρμαίρω ‘to flash, sparkle, gleam’ (said of any darting, quivering light).

text: 131. Byangsi śiṅram ‘ginger’, Chaudangsi ɕin-rəm ‘ginger’, Darma ɕiŋ-wəm ‘ginger’ and perhaps Chepang sim.phərʔ ‘ginger’ are most certainly not borrowings from OIA śr̥ṅgavera- ‘dried or fresh ginger’ (12588). Turner (CDIAL) and Mayrhofer (EWA) speculate about Dravidian connections (which is correct for -vera- which cf. with Tam. vēr ‘root’) and ultimate borrowing of a (South-)East Asian culture word. Yet, the Austro-Asiatic origin is quite obvious: Khasi sʔíːŋ ‘ginger’, Tˈin khɨːŋ ‘ginger’, Bolyu tɕiŋ⁵⁵ ‘ginger’, Riang kᵊsiaŋ¹ ‘ginger (Zingiber officinale)’ and Danaw kᵊʦɑŋ⁴ ‘ginger (Zingiber officinale)’ and Palaung siaŋ ‘ginger’, and Proto-Vietic *s-gəːŋ ‘ginger’. Byangsi -ram and Chaudangsi -rəm are the same as Darma rɯm ‘root’. Thus, the WH and the OIA forms have the same semantic structure ‘ginger-root’. Darma -wəm compares with Western Tani amya ‘root’ and different variants of the Zeme Group which have forms like ama, küman, pema all ‘root’ which suggest that WH -rəm, rɯm is basically a synonym compound ‘root-root’ with -r- perhaps related with Proto- Karenic #7445 PKar *rwiB ‘root’.

text: 106. Pr. ẓugˈo ‘bell’, ẓugˈeig ‘bell; rushing or roaring of water’, ẓuṅulˈeig ‘small bell’ appear etymologically related with Kal. gạṅgạí ‘large bell (typically tied to the neck of a male goat or bull)’. We deal here obviously with ideophones for which *gruṅ-, *groṅ-, *graṅ- can be reconstructed — Nuristani Kt. gřaṅˈaři ‘bell’ — West Himalayish Bun. koroŋkoroŋ ‘a bell’ and Darma kɔloŋ ‘bell (a type)’, and also Bodo gugrá ‘bell (kind of, round, tied to the neck of a horse)’ is almost identical with below Santali. The forms are ultimately borrowings from Austro-Asiatic: — Sant. ghugra ‘morris bells, a band of small bells tied round the ankles when dancing’ and here perhaps also ghanar ghunur ‘tinkling, jingling (sound of small bells)’, Korku ghuruŋgula, guruŋgula ‘string of small bells worn by bullocks’ and koɽoŋ ‘round brass bell for cattle’ — Bahnar grɛŋ- nɛŋ ‘small bell’ and Cua graneŋ ∼ gareŋ ∼ reŋ ‘bell’, Halang gəgraʔ gəgri̤ːŋ ‘jingling of bells’ and griːŋ ‘the rings of a small bell’, Sre gruŋ ‘bell’, Ngeq krlooŋ ‘buffalo bell’, Khmu krlɛːŋ ‘metal bell around an animal’s neck’, Thavung kalɛŋ ‘a small cylindrically shape bell’, etc. Note: Derivation of the the Pr. and Kal. form < OIA *ghuṅghura- ‘bell’ (4477), for which Turner suggests borrowing from Dravidian which he supports by quot- ing Kan. gugguri ‘curl’, is unlikely. Here more or less (in)directly connected are also the following: H. ghanghan- ‘(bell) sound, jingle, clink’, OIA *ghanaghana- ‘tinkle, clang’ (4425) which is according to Turner and Mayrhofer onomatopoeic.
